# Keep michi-pipeline small, record-centric, and replay-honest

The best-practice design for an in-process, embeddable Tokio step pipeline is a static DAG of steps with stable, caller-chosen string ids, validated in full before anything runs. It has one scheduler loop over a `JoinSet` with a concurrency cap, and it returns an immutable per-run record in which every step has exactly one terminal status and a reason. It resumes by skipping steps the record says definitively succeeded, under the same run id, so a `run_id:step_id` idempotency key stays stable for downstream deduplication. The proposed redesign already gets most of this right. `ExecStep` with ids and `depends_on`, a single `execute()` with a `Mode`, a caller-supplied `RunId`, `StepContext` with `idempotency_key() = run_id:step_id`, a returned `RunRecord`, reasoned statuses, and resume-from-record all match what Temporal, Step Functions, Dagster, Argo, Tekton, GitHub Actions and the provenance literature converge on. Where it falls short is at the edges. It has no status for a step that was cancelled or timed out mid-flight, which is ambiguous, not "skipped". It does not say what resume does with a step whose prior outcome was ambiguous. It does not bind resume to the same plan through a fingerprint. It keeps one circuit breaker for the whole pipeline. It has no per-step progress hook, so a crash mid-run loses the whole record. On build versus adopt, the honest result is that the world-class pieces michi needs are mostly already present (tokio `JoinSet`, `tokio::time`, michi-core's retry math). The one clear new adoption is tokio-util's `CancellationToken`. tower, petgraph, retry crates and breaker crates fail on fit, not quality, because michi's distinctive value is the replay-safety classification that those generic crates do not model.

Verification convention used below: claims with a source link were read in a primary source by the researchers unless marked **[unverified]**. That tag carries over the notes' [K], [prior] and "Unverified" labels for items that were cited from background knowledge and not re-fetched. Statements framed as recommendations, or prefixed "inference", are reasoning rather than sourced fact.

## Stable string ids, not handles or UUIDs, are the identity everyone converges on

Every orchestrator surveyed gives a step a caller-chosen identity that is unique within the definition and separate from its display name. GitHub Actions requires `job_id` to match `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_-]*` and treats `name` as display-only ([GitHub workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax)). Argo keys nodes by ID with a separate `DisplayName` ([Argo workflow_types.go](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-workflows/main/pkg/apis/workflow/v1alpha1/workflow_types.go)). An Airflow task instance is "a specific run of that task for a given Dag" ([Airflow tasks](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/core-concepts/tasks.html)). The libraries closest to michi's resume use case key memoization on **stable, user-chosen strings**. Inngest's `step.run(id, …)` id "is used to memoize step state across function versions" ([Inngest](https://www.inngest.com/docs/reference/functions/step-run)), and Prefect restores prior completed state on a cache-key match ([Prefect tasks](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/develop/write-tasks)). Bevy uses typed labels instead, so misspellings are compile errors ([bevy SystemSet](https://docs.rs/bevy/latest/bevy/ecs/schedule/trait.SystemSet.html)), but its systems are static code, and no measured evidence was found that typed handles reduce errors in pipeline libraries.

The proposed `ExecStep{id, name, …}` is therefore correct. Two refinements follow. First, wrap ids in `StepId`/`RunId` newtypes, per the Rust API Guidelines' C-NEWTYPE ("Newtypes provide static distinctions") ([API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/checklist.html)). Second, validate a charset and length so ids stay short and copyable by agents. Anthropic reports that replacing arbitrary UUIDs with semantically meaningful identifiers "significantly improves Claude's precision in retrieval tasks by reducing hallucinations" ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)). One practitioner team found a UUID costs about 10 tokens and that "the more UUIDs in the prompt, the higher the error rate", though without measured rates ([Dexter](https://engineering.getdexter.co/2026/03/10/short-ids-for-llms/)). The same logic applies to `RunId`. If an agent has to echo it back to resume, a short semantic form beats a raw UUID. Better still, the host keeps the run implicit and maps "resume" to it.

The idempotency key format has direct precedent. Temporal recommends "a combination of the Workflow Run ID and the Activity ID as an idempotency key… consistent across retry attempts but unique among Workflow Executions", enforced "by the service you are calling… not by the Activity itself" ([Temporal](https://docs.temporal.io/activity-definition)). Beldi logs operations keyed by instance ID plus step number **[unverified]** ([Beldi](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi20-zhang_haoran.pdf)). AWS's client tokens are reused across retries, and reusing a token with different parameters is a validation error ([AWS Builders' Library](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/)). So `attempt` must stay out of the key, as the proposal has it. `attempt` stays in `StepContext` for logging and backoff only. One caution is inference: michi cannot deduplicate two starts that use the same `RunId`, so the docs should state what happens if a caller reuses one for a different plan or inputs. That is AWS's "same token, different parameters" hazard.

## The definition is a plan and the run record is the only thing that changes

All eight orchestrators surveyed separate an immutable definition from a per-run record, and none mutates the definition during a run. Examples are Step Functions' versioned machine versus execution ARN ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html)), Tekton's Pipeline versus PipelineRun ([Tekton](https://tekton.dev/docs/pipelines/pipelineruns/)), and Prefect's definitions versus run states ([Prefect states](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/states)). W3C PROV draws the same line. A _Plan_ is "a set of actions or steps intended by one or more agents to achieve some goals", and an _Activity_ is "something that occurs over a period of time" ([PROV-DM](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/)). Provenance research calls these prospective and retrospective provenance ([Ragan et al.](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~aendert3/resources/ragan-vast-2015.pdf)). The proposal's move from a mutated reusable definition to a returned `RunRecord` is the single most important correction in the redesign.

The record should be a plain value, serializable under the existing `serde` feature, with persistence left to the caller (inference). Its minimum contents, drawn from the industry survey, are: `run_id`; per step a terminal status with a reason, the attempt count with per-attempt classification, timing, and the error; a derived overall outcome; and a **plan fingerprint** over `(id, depends_on)`. The fingerprint is what lets resume reject a drifted plan. Step Functions requires that you "must start a new execution if you update your state machine definition" ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html)). Dagster requires re-executed step keys to be consistent with the parent plan ([Dagster execution API](https://docs.dagster.io/_modules/dagster/_core/execution/api)). Nextflow invalidates its cache when hashed inputs change ([Nextflow](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/cache-and-resume)). Closures cannot be hashed, so structure is the practical stand-in (inference). Keep `RunRecord` fields private behind accessors (C-STRUCT-PRIVATE) and mark it `#[must_use]`.

Data passing deserves a deliberate non-decision. Dataflow systems pass outputs, and once resume exists that forces serialization. Inngest JSON-serializes every return value, so a `Date` comes back as a string ([Inngest](https://www.inngest.com/docs/reference/functions/step-run)). Dagster's resume-from-failure "requires an I/O manager that can access outputs from other runs" ([Dagster run retries](https://docs.dagster.io/deployment/run-retries)). Concurrency utilities like errgroup carry no outputs ([errgroup](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup)). For michi, side-effect-only steps (`Result<(), …>`) with state shared through `Arc` captures is the right default. If anything flows into the record, it should be a small optional summary for agent display, not an input to downstream steps (inference).

## A status model built around recovery verbs, not lifecycle phases

Production status models are large because they cover distributed lifecycles: Airflow has fourteen task states and Prefect twenty ([Prefect states](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/states)). Most of those (scheduled, queued, deferred, late, removed) mean nothing in-process. Three distinctions recur that do matter. First, **skips must never let a run read as succeeded**. Tekton reports `Completed` rather than `Succeeded` when "one or more Tasks were skipped" ([Tekton](https://tekton.dev/docs/pipelines/pipelineruns/)), and GitHub Actions' skipped-as-success behaviour lets required checks pass despite upstream failure ([Jake Wharton](https://jakewharton.com/fan-in-to-a-single-required-github-action/), [actions/runner#491](https://github.com/actions/runner/issues/491)). Second, **harness failure is distinct from step failure**. Argo separates `Failed` ("non-zero code") from `Error` ("error other than a non-zero exit code") ([Argo types](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-workflows/main/pkg/apis/workflow/v1alpha1/workflow_types.go)), and Prefect separates `Crashed` from `Failed` ([Prefect states](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/states)). Third, **timeouts are a distinct outcome**, as in GitHub's `timed_out` conclusion ([GitHub check runs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs)) and Temporal's per-type timeouts ([Temporal failures](https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/detecting-activity-failures)).

The proposed reasons all have analogues except one. `Skipped(PrerequisiteFailed)` matches Airflow `upstream_failed` and Argo `Omitted`. `Skipped(Cancelled)` matches GitHub and Tekton cancellation. `CompletedEarlier` matches Prefect `Cached` and Step Functions redrive keeping successes. `NotRun(CircuitOpen)` has no direct analogue, but it is correct. An open breaker fails fast without calling the operation **[unverified]** ([Fowler](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html)), so nothing ran, the step is safe to run on resume, and it should not count as a failed attempt.

The gap is the mid-flight case. A step that was running when the run was cancelled, or when its timeout dropped its future, may have performed its effect. Under RFC 9110 that is exactly a "communication failure … before the client is able to read the server's response" ([RFC 9110 §9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2)). It belongs with ambiguous outcomes, not with `Skipped(Cancelled)`, which should mean "cancelled before start". The redesign should add an explicit `Failed(Ambiguous{cause: Timeout | Cancelled | Transport})` (or `OutcomeUnknown`) terminal status. Two more additions round out the model: a `Panicked` or harness-error reason distinct from a step's own error, and an overall verdict that cannot be `Succeeded` when any step is skipped, not run or ambiguous (inference built on the sources above). Following conc's observation that errors after cancellation are mostly noise ([conc pool](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/sourcegraph/conc/pool)), the record should separate the **root-cause** failure from consequential skips. Then an agent sees one cause, not N errors. Each reason should map one-to-one to a recovery verb an agent can act on: retry, verify then resume, fix input, or no action. That is Anthropic's "specific and actionable" guidance applied to statuses ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)). Mark `StepStatus` and every reason enum `#[non_exhaustive]`.

## Resume is forward recovery, at least once per step, and must respect ambiguity

michi's four-way replay classification is a near-literal implementation of RFC 9110 §9.2.2. Idempotent requests "can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs". A client "SHOULD NOT automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent … or some means to detect that the original request was never applied" ([RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.2)). Not-executed is the "never applied" case. Ambiguous (timeout, 502, 504) is the communication-failure case. One caveat is inference: treating 429 and 503 as "not applied" is a widespread convention, not an RFC guarantee. §15.6.4 defines 503 only as temporary overload ([RFC 9110 §15.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.6)), and an intermediary's 503 could mask partial application, so the docs should state the assumption and let steps override it. Gating ambiguous retries on idempotency is **stricter than every orchestrator surveyed** (inference). Temporal says activities "may be executed more than once… may even partially complete more than once" and retries anyway, leaving idempotency to the author ([Temporal](https://docs.temporal.io/activity-definition)). Airflow tells authors to replace INSERT with UPSERT ([Airflow best practices](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/best-practices.html)). michi's rule is a genuine differentiator for agent tools and should be kept.

Resume in the proposal is what the build-systems literature calls a **dirty-bit rebuilder**, where dirty means "not definitively succeeded in record R". The scheduler and the rebuilder are independent axes: "a 'scheduler'" can be "cleanly separated from" the part that decides "whether a key needs to be rebuilt" ([Build Systems à la Carte](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2018/03/build-systems.pdf)). It is not input-sensitive. A step whose inputs changed between runs would be wrongly skipped, and input-sensitive skipping needs verifying traces and determinism, which belong to build systems, not michi. The docs should say plainly that resume continues an interrupted run and is not incremental recomputation. It is also saga-style forward recovery from save-points ([Sagas](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/andru/cs711/2002fa/reading/sagas.pdf)), with each completed step serving as a save-point.

Durable-execution research sets the ceiling. Durable Functions proves observably exactly-once execution only because "the storage system [provides] an atomic commit mechanism", and even then "external calls can be duplicated if there are multiple attempts at executing a work item" ([Durable Functions](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2021/10/DF-Semantics-Final.pdf)). michi has no atomic commit between "the effect happened" and "the record says so". Resume is therefore **at least once per step**, and effects are exactly-once only when the step passes `idempotency_key()` to a deduplicating downstream. That is the end-to-end argument **[unverified]** ([Saltzer, Reed & Clark](https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/endtoend/endtoend.pdf)). Never claim exactly-once. There is an advantage over Temporal and Durable Functions here: the orchestration is the static DAG, deterministic by construction, so users carry no replay-determinism burden (inference).

Four resume rules follow, and the proposal states none of them. **Keep the same `RunId`**, as Step Functions redrive (same ARN), GitHub re-runs (same SHA and ref) and the key's stability all require ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html), [GitHub re-runs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/re-run-workflows-and-jobs)). A fresh id defeats downstream deduplication. **Reject plan drift** with the fingerprint. **Treat a prior ambiguous step as ambiguous again**: re-invoke it only if it is idempotent, otherwise surface it for reconciliation, because treating ambiguous as not-done turns resume back into blind replay. **Never implicitly re-run completed steps.** Step Functions' rerun of successful branches on `States.DataLimitExceeded` is a documented pitfall ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html)). To survive a process crash rather than just returned errors, callers need to persist progress incrementally. A per-step-completion observer callback is the minimal embeddable affordance for that (inference).

Retry policy should follow the cross-source consensus. Use bounded attempts with randomized exponential backoff, and retry at **one layer only**: 3 retries across 5 layers is about 243x load ([AWS](https://builder.aws.com/content/3EumjoZascWd1oZiEgL8ORlv3qE/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter)), and the SRE book warns against "issuing retries at multiple levels" ([SRE ch. 22](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)). Budget retries too. The SRE book allows retries only while the retry ratio is "below 10%", which holds load growth to about 1.1x versus "just below 3X" with per-request caps alone ([SRE ch. 21](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)). tower's `TpsBudget` implements the same idea, warning "It's generally dangerous to implement retries without some limiting factor" ([tower budget](https://docs.rs/tower/latest/tower/retry/budget/index.html)). Temporal recommends bounding retries by a total Schedule-To-Close timeout rather than attempts ([Temporal retry policies](https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/retry-policies)), which argues for both a per-attempt timeout and a total step budget. Compensation fits only definitive failures after earlier effects commit, and the Sagas paper admits a failing compensation leaves "the system … stuck" ([Sagas](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/andru/cs711/2002fa/reading/sagas.pdf)). A saga coordinator is out of scope. Listing definitively succeeded steps in completion order in the record lets callers compensate themselves.

## One scheduler loop, a slot cap, cooperative cancellation, and negligible overhead

Every task-graph system surveyed runs the same loop. It keeps a remaining-dependency count per node, pushes newly ready dependents into a queue, and pops while a slot is free. Cargo's job queue "must not spawn more than N threads of work" and calls its own prioritization "relatively rudimentary" ([Cargo job_queue](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/master/src/compiler/job_queue/mod.rs)). Its std-only `DependencyQueue` (remaining-deps map, reverse-deps map, priority) is the best design reference ([dependency_queue.rs](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/master/src/util/dependency_queue.rs)). Kahn's ready-queue algorithm is O(V+E) and detects cycles **[unverified]** ([Kahn 1962](https://doi.org/10.1145/368996.369025)). Any greedy list schedule is within (2 − 1/m) of optimal makespan **[unverified]** ([Graham 1969](https://doi.org/10.1137/0117039)), and critical-path heuristics need durations michi does not have **[unverified]** ([Kwok & Ahmad](https://doi.org/10.1145/344588.344618)). A FIFO ready queue with ties broken by declaration order is therefore sufficient, and it makes records reproducible. Because `depends_on` is static, this topological scheduler is the right one. Dynamic dependencies would need a restarting or suspending scheduler ([Build Systems à la Carte](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2018/03/build-systems.pdf)) and should be an explicit non-goal.

The proposal's single `execute()` with `Mode` is right. Inference: implement `Sequential` as the same loop with a cap of one and deterministic declaration-order dispatch. That removes the divergence between today's two executors, and it satisfies the industry note's point that sequential mode needs deterministic ordering, not merely a cap of one. Use `Parallel{max_concurrency: NonZeroUsize}`, since errgroup documents the `SetLimit(0)` hazard that a zero cap creates ([errgroup](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup)). The cap belongs in the dispatch loop (`while in_flight < max`), not in a `Semaphore` inside spawned tasks, which would park spawned tasks and admit them in wake order (inference). Current michi already uses `JoinSet` with no cap. `JoinSet` is the right primitive: it aborts all tasks on drop, surfaces a panic as `JoinError`, and `join_next` is cancel-safe ([JoinSet](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/struct.JoinSet.html)). So no step outlives `execute()`, and a panicking step becomes a step failure rather than unwinding the executor. `FuturesUnordered`/`buffer_unordered` lose panic isolation and want a stream known up front **[unverified]**.

Failure policy needs a name. Turborepo offers `--continue=never` (cancel all), `dependencies-successful` (cancel only dependents) and `always` ([Turborepo](https://turborepo.dev/docs/reference/run)). Cargo's fail-fast stops scheduling and then waits "for pending work to finish" ([Cargo](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/master/src/compiler/job_queue/mod.rs)). Structured concurrency defaults to cancelling siblings on failure ([N. J. Smith](https://vorpus.org/blog/notes-on-structured-concurrency-or-go-statement-considered-harmful/)), but JEP 505 makes the policy pluggable, including an `awaitAll` that "simply waits for all subtasks to complete" ([JEP 505](https://openjdk.org/jeps/505)). For a DAG, the right default is to continue independent branches and skip transitive dependents. `FailFast` is opt-in (inference). Fail-fast should cancel the run token, drain until a grace deadline, and then `abort_all`, recording unstarted steps as `Skipped(Cancelled)` and in-flight ones as ambiguous. Backoff sleeps should `select!` on cancellation. Following SRE deadline propagation ([SRE ch. 22](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)), `StepContext` should carry the run's child cancellation token and remaining deadline.

Circuit breaker scope is the main performance-and-correctness defect in the current design. One breaker shared by all steps lets one failing dependency trip unrelated steps. Envoy keeps failure counters per upstream host ([Envoy FAQ](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.9.0/faq/transient_failures)), and resilience4j/Polly name instances per downstream **[unverified]**. Use a breaker registry keyed by an optional step-declared `breaker_key`, long-lived across runs because a single run produces few samples (inference). Overhead is not a concern: tokio task overhead measured informally is "at most 50ns" ([alamb](https://github.com/alamb/rust_tokio_overhead)), so 500 steps cost well under a millisecond against millisecond-to-second step latencies (inference). The real performance risks are uncapped fan-out, retry amplification and idle slots, and the cap, the budget and the keyed breaker address all three. `max_concurrency` doubles as a bulkhead.

## Ease of use comes from one validation pass, closures, and paused-clock tests

Of the libraries examined, the common shape separates what a step does (closure or trait), how it is retried (a policy value), and when it runs (dependency declaration) ([tower](https://docs.rs/tower/latest/tower/), [Temporal](https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/retry-policies), [Prefect](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/develop/write-tasks)). `ExecStep{runner}` plus options fits this. Temporal and Prefect both configure retries per activity, so a per-step retry override should be available. Validation is where today's michi is weakest. `depends_on(&str, &str)` returns `()` and defers unknown ids and cycles to execute time (local source, `crates/michi-pipeline/src/lib.rs`). dagrs returns `Result<Graph, DagrsError>` at build time ([dagrs](https://docs.rs/dagrs/latest/dagrs/)). michi should run one pass that rejects unknown dependencies, duplicates, self-dependencies and cycles, and returns **all** violations, not just the first. An invalid plan must come back as `Result::Err` before execution, so it cannot be confused with a run that happened and failed. Exposing that pass as `plan(&steps, &opts) -> Result<Plan, PlanError>` gives agents a cheap dry-run preview and makes validation testable on its own (inference). For MCP, step failures go in an `isError: true` tool result, not a protocol error, with structured content duplicated as text ([MCP tools](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools)). Default rendering should be concise: non-completed steps plus a `completed: 7/10` count, with a detailed mode available, following Anthropic's response-format pattern.

Two small API-guideline points apply. C-CUSTOM-TYPE argues against meaning-carrying bools, so `is_idempotent() -> bool` reads better as `fn replay(&self) -> Replay { Unsafe, Idempotent }` ([API Guidelines](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/checklist.html)). Resume should be a separate `resume(&RunRecord, …)` entry point, or an explicit options field, not a positional `Option<&RunRecord>`. Testability comes nearly free. `#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]` auto-advances the clock "to the next pending timer" when idle ([tokio pause](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/time/fn.pause.html)), making backoff, timeouts and breaker windows instant, as long as michi uses `tokio::time` throughout and jitter stays injectable through the existing seed. The cap is tested with an in-flight high-water mark, fail-fast by asserting virtual elapsed time, and resume by running, editing the record, and resuming. That last test needs `RunRecord` to be a value type with public read accessors. loom, turmoil and madsim add little here (inference).

## The redesign's divergences cluster at the edges, not the core

Inside an embeddable library the line against orchestrator creep is clear. Per-run concurrency transfers. Airflow pools, GitHub concurrency groups and Argo semaphores are cross-run and need a server, and even Dagster's concurrency limits are "only applied on a per-run basis" ([Dagster](https://dagster.io/docs/guides/build/jobs/job-execution)). Scheduling, persistence servers, UIs, event-history replay, cross-process workers, dynamic dependencies, trigger-rule languages, compensation, input-hash memoization and critical-path priorities all belong to orchestrators or build systems. Each would trade michi's main selling point, being a small library that renders agent-legible results, for features its users get elsewhere. The opinionated layer worth building is narrow: the replay classification, the reasoned status model, idempotency keys, resume semantics, and agent-facing rendering.

Measured against that, the proposal diverges from best practice in seven places. It conflates mid-flight cancellation with not-started cancellation and has no ambiguous terminal status. It leaves resume's treatment of prior ambiguous steps undefined. It has no plan fingerprint and does not state that resume must reuse the `RunId`. It keeps a single pipeline-wide breaker. It has no retry budget and no total per-step time budget. It has no per-step completion hook, so the record is lost on crash. It does not specify an all-violations validation pass that is separate from execution results, or the failure policy for independent branches. The remaining items are hygiene: an overall verdict that is never `Succeeded` with skips, a harness-versus-step failure split, `NonZeroUsize`, `#[non_exhaustive]`, newtyped ids, and an enum in place of the idempotency bool.

## Conclusion

The research shifts the framing of the redesign. The hard problem is not scheduling, which is solved, cheap and well served by tokio. It is being honest about what a step's outcome means once processes, timeouts and cancellation intervene. michi's RFC 9110-grounded refusal to auto-retry ambiguous non-idempotent work is stricter than Temporal, Airflow or Step Functions, and that strictness is the product. The redesign should extend it consistently to cancellation, timeouts and resume rather than letting those paths quietly reintroduce blind replay. Build-versus-adopt confirms the principle in an unexpected way: "adopt world-class pieces" mostly means trusting the tokio michi already uses, adding tokio-util, and resisting tower and petgraph whose abstractions would dissolve the typed replay model.

Ranked changes to the proposed redesign:

1. Add an ambiguous terminal status (`Failed(Ambiguous{Timeout | Cancelled | Transport})`). Restrict `Skipped(Cancelled)` to steps never started. Record in-flight cancellation and timeout of non-idempotent steps as ambiguous.
2. Define resume semantics explicitly. It reuses the prior `RunId`, rejects a mismatched plan fingerprint over `(id, depends_on)`, re-invokes prior ambiguous steps only if idempotent (otherwise it surfaces them), never re-runs `CompletedEarlier` steps, and is documented as at-least-once, not incremental recomputation.
3. Replace the pipeline-wide breaker with a registry keyed by an optional per-step `breaker_key`, reusable across runs, and add a run-scoped retry budget in michi-core plus a per-step total time budget.
4. Validate the whole plan before running (unknown, duplicate and self dependencies, cycles), return all violations as `Err(PlanError)` separate from `RunRecord`, and expose it as a dry-run `plan()`.
5. Implement one scheduler loop on `JoinSet` with `Parallel{max_concurrency: NonZeroUsize}`, `Sequential` as cap 1 with declaration-order dispatch, and a named `FailurePolicy` defaulting to continue-independent with opt-in `FailFast` (cancel, drain to grace, `abort_all`).
6. Adopt tokio-util `CancellationToken` behind michi's newtype, and put a child token and remaining deadline on `StepContext`.
7. Add a per-step completion observer so callers can persist the record incrementally and survive crashes.
8. Make the overall verdict never read `Succeeded` with skipped, not-run or ambiguous steps. Separate harness failures (panic) from step errors, and the root cause from consequential skips.
9. Apply type hygiene: `StepId`/`RunId` newtypes with a short-slug charset, `#[non_exhaustive]` status and reason enums, a `Replay` enum in place of `is_idempotent() -> bool`, a separate `resume()` entry point, and a `#[must_use]` `RunRecord` with private fields and serde behind the feature.

# Architecture

This document describes how the `michi` workspace crates fit together.

## Workspace Layout

`michi` is structured as a virtual Cargo workspace (the root `Cargo.toml` has no `[package]`) with two published crates in `crates/` and one unpublished binding crate in `packages/`:

```text
michi (workspace root, virtual manifest)
├── crates/
│   ├── michi-core        # Every sync primitive: toon, kv, hints, recovery, empty, error, status, mcp, audience,
│   │                     #   response (AgentResponse), pipeline (data type), truncate, resilience, telemetry; napi (feature)
│   └── michi-pipeline    # Async pipeline execution: Plan, execute/resume, RunRecord, BreakerRegistry, CancellationToken
└── packages/michi-node   # Node.js NAPI cdylib (@orin-dx/michi), publish = false
```

Dependency direction:

```mermaid
graph LR
    core["michi-core"]
    pipeline["michi-pipeline"]
    node["packages/michi-node (@orin-dx/michi)"]

    pipeline --> core
    node -- "features = [napi]" --> core
```

All three version in lockstep (each crate's `version`, kept equal by Callisto), released together as a Callisto fixed group. `michi-pipeline` and `michi-node` depend on `michi-core` through an exact `=x.y.z` workspace pin, so a mixed set never resolves.

## Component Overview

| Crate / Package | Responsibility | Runtime Dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `michi-core` | All sync AXI primitives. `toon`: TOON list rendering and parsing with stack-inlined `CompactString` cells. `truncate`: UTF-8 char-boundary content truncation (`floor_char_boundary`). `resilience`: retry back-off math, `Retry-After` HTTP date parsing, FNV-1a idempotency keys. Response DTOs: `AgentResponse`, `DomainError`, `StatusResponse`, `CallToolResult`, and the `Pipeline` data type. `resilience::*` and `truncate::*` are re-exported at the crate root. | `thiserror`, `compact_str` (Optional: `serde`, `serde_json`, `schemars`, `miette`, `napi`, `napi-derive`) |
| `michi-pipeline` | Async execution of a validated `Plan` of steps: one `JoinSet` scheduler (sequential or capped parallel), a returned `RunRecord` whose statuses are `michi-core`'s `StepStatus`, `resume` from a record, a keyed `BreakerRegistry`, a per-run `RetryBudget`, `CancellationToken` and a `StepObserver`. Own `ExecutionError` and `PlanError` types, converting into `DomainError` via `From` — not variants of `michi_core::Error`. See `docs/spec/08-pipeline-execution.md`. | `michi-core`, `tokio`, `tokio-util`, `thiserror` (optional: `serde`) |
| `packages/michi-node` | NAPI cdylib shim for `@orin-dx/michi`. Not published to crates.io. | `michi-core` (`napi` feature), `napi`, `napi-derive` |

## Data Composition & Render Flow

`michi` provides two main entry points for formatting output:

1. **`response::AgentResponse` (Fluent Builder)**: Composes TOON lists, KV items, `help[]` hints, and recovery guidance into a unified output buffer. Supports assistant/user audience routing and direct conversion to MCP `CallToolResult`.
2. **Standalone DTOs**: `DomainError`, `StatusResponse`, `AlreadyDone`, and `empty_state()` render themselves directly into agent-readable KV blocks or GitHub Actions annotations without passing through `AgentResponse`.

## Node.js / NAPI Bridge (`packages/michi-node`)

The Node.js native addon lives in `packages/michi-node` because Cargo requires a separate `cdylib` target definition:

- Public FFI exports, input validation, and bounds checking live in `crates/michi-core/src/napi.rs` (numeric newtypes in `napi/num.rs`), compiled only with `michi-core`'s `napi` feature.
- `packages/michi-node/src/lib.rs` re-exports those functions across the crate boundary via `pub use michi_core::napi::*;`.
- `napi-derive` uses linker sections (`ctor`) to register native functions across crate boundaries without manual wrapper boilerplates.

## NAPI Boundary Contract

The NAPI boundary (`crates/michi-core/src/napi.rs`) has a specific constructor discipline that differs from pure-Rust callers:

**NAPI functions always use normalizing constructors (`new()`), never strict ones (`try_new()`).**

- `RetryConfig::new()` normalizes out-of-range inputs silently (clamps `jitter_factor`, floors `max_delay`, etc.). `napi.rs`'s resilience-domain call sites use it this way; making it fallible there would require either `unwrap()`/`expect()` (banned) or a silent fallback to `Default` (defeats validation).
- Pure-Rust callers and tests may use `try_new()` / `validate()` for explicit error signals.
- JS-facing functions report errors via `napi::Error`, not `Result` propagation — validation that can't be normalized (truly invalid JS input) becomes a JS exception at the boundary, not a Rust panic.

This asymmetry is intentional. The NAPI layer operates in a "be maximally resilient to JS input, fail loudly only for truly unrecoverable cases" mode; the Rust library layer operates in a "signal problems explicitly through types" mode.

**Error output path:** When you hold a `DomainError`, call `domain_error.to_call_tool_result()` directly. Do not wrap it in `AgentResponse::as_error()` — that double-wraps the render and loses the typed `error`/`retryable` fields from `structured_content`. Both `AgentResponse::to_call_tool_result()` and `DomainError::to_call_tool_result()` produce structurally compatible `structured_content` JSON (same top-level keys).

# Root-cause analysis: `edge-cases.md` findings

Phase 0 of the edge-case remediation effort. Four parallel agents each took a candidate cluster from `edge-cases.md` and asked not "what's broken" (already catalogued) but "what's missing that let it happen" — reading the actual code at every cited site, not just trusting the audit's summary. Three of the four found their assigned cluster wasn't one mechanism, it was several; after splitting, **11 confirmed mechanism-level root causes** and **7 genuinely standalone findings** remain.

**The overall pattern:** this codebase has good conventions in places that got established once — a named constructor, a depth counter, a truncation helper, a documented precedence order — but nothing makes those conventions load-bearing. They're advisory, so a parallel or later code path silently diverges from them. The fix shape repeats across clusters: turn an advisory helper into the _only_ callable constructor, or add the one missing signal channel a class of code was never given. Two clusters (panic containment, schema derivation) are genuinely new architectural decisions and get an ADR; the rest are internal refactors of an existing-but-unenforced pattern.

**Adversarially verified 2026-08-04:** every root-cause diagnosis in this document was independently re-checked against the actual current source by a second, skeptical pass (7 agents, defaulting to refute). All diagnoses held up — no fabricated citations, no stale line numbers. Two mechanisms as originally drafted were **unsound** (would not compile, or would not stop the misuse they targeted) and have been rewritten below; several others were underspecified in ways an implementer would trip on and have been corrected inline, marked **[corrected]**. Where a correction narrows scope or changes the fix shape, the original claim is noted so the reasoning is traceable.

---

## Mechanism clusters

### 1. Resolver give-up constructor discipline `[corrected]`

**Root cause (narrowed on verification):** the original claim — "6 of ~10 `Opaque` construction sites bypass the named constructor" — overstated the blast radius. Verification found only **3 sites genuinely silent**: `func.rs:61` (`MultiParamFunction`, zero diagnostic anywhere nearby), `chain.rs:40` (cycle-detected `ResolvedChain::default()`, zero diagnostic), `alias.rs:116` (`LiteralUnion`-as-props-base, zero diagnostic, unlike the parallel diagnosed path at `alias.rs:234-253`). The two other sites originally named as bypassing the pattern — `primitives.rs:181` and `template.rs:39` — actually already push a correctly-shaped `Diagnostic` immediately before constructing the `Opaque`; they just don't call `collected.rs`'s helper, which is a private `fn` and structurally can't be called from those files today anyway. That's a duplication/style gap, not a silent-failure bug — don't conflate it with the real 3.

**Mechanism (rewritten — the original was unsound):** the original proposal — make `ResolvedChain`'s bare/`Default` construction private, and restructure `PropType::Opaque { raw, reason }` into a tuple variant `Opaque(OpaqueDetail)` with the only public constructor being a diagnostic-emitting `give_up()` — does not work, for two independent reasons verified against the real code:

1. **Reverse-dependency violation.** `known.rs` owns roughly 7 of the real `PropType::Opaque` construction sites and is required by `AGENTS.md`'s "no reverse dependencies" rule to never depend on `resolver::ResolveState`. A `give_up(state: &mut ResolveState, ...)` signature as the _only_ public constructor can't be called from `known.rs` at all. This split is intentional and already tested (`test_known_opaque_result_emits_diagnostic`, `test_known_opaque_result_emits_diagnostic_at_chain_level`): `known.rs` constructs the bare value, the _caller_ (`chain.rs`/`named.rs`) diagnoses it via `push_known_opaque_diagnostic` using context `known.rs` doesn't have. Collapsing construction and diagnosis into one constructor breaks this tested split. `types/output.rs`'s hand-written `Deserialize` impl also constructs `PropType::Opaque{..}` twice, reconstructing from wire JSON with no `ResolveState` in scope at all — deserialization isn't a give-up event and the original plan never accounted for it.
2. **`ResolvedChain` privacy is close to a non-issue, and harmful if forced.** The struct and its fields are already private to the `resolver` module tree — unreachable from outside `resolver/` today. Within `resolver/`, `chain.rs`, `alias.rs`, `named.rs`, and `extends.rs` all have _equal_ access to `resolver::mod.rs`'s private items — Rust's privacy model can't distinguish `chain.rs:40`'s illegitimate give-up call from `alias.rs`'s ~9 _legitimate_ accumulator-init call sites (later filled by `chain.merge_parent(...)` in a loop) at the same privacy tier. Only 1 of the 11 bare/`Default()` construction sites found is actually a silent give-up; the rest are legitimate accumulator seeds, deliberately-silent non-error short-circuits, or success-path struct-update literals. Forcing all of them through one diagnostic-emitting constructor would spuriously diagnose non-error paths.

**Corrected mechanism:** scope the fix to exactly the 3 confirmed sites. Add a small helper — callable wherever `ResolveState` is already in scope, which all 3 sites qualify for — e.g. `ResolvedChain::give_up(type_name: String, diag: Option<Diagnostic>, state: &mut ResolveState) -> Self` used _only_ at `chain.rs:40`, and an equivalent minimal fix at `func.rs:61` and `alias.rs:116` (push the missing diagnostic inline, matching the shape `alias.rs:234-253` already uses — doesn't need a new type). Leave `known.rs`'s construct-then-caller-diagnoses split untouched — it's correct and tested. Leave `ResolvedChain`'s and `PropType::Opaque`'s existing construction surface as-is; do not attempt to make either "give-up-only-constructible."

**Resolves:** `resolver-chain-cycle-detected-default`, `resolver-func-multiparam-no-diagnostic`, `resolver-literalunion-as-props-base` (P2 items in `edge-cases.md`).

**ADR:** No — enforcing an existing pattern, not introducing a new one.

### 2. Extractor missing give-up signal channel

**Root cause:** `classify_type_alias`, `extract_type_name_from_type`, and the component-detector `.or_else()` chains in `visit.rs` are `Option`-returning `?`-chains over AST shapes with no way to distinguish "wrong shape, fine" from "matched but malformed, worth flagging." `SourceData.diagnostics` exists and other extractor code already pushes into it (nesting-depth guard, parse errors) — it was simply never wired to these specific functions. This is a design gap, not helper drift: no helper could be "used inconsistently" because none was ever built for this call shape.

**Mechanism:** Add `fn record_skip(&mut self, code: DiagnosticCode, message: impl Into<String>, span: Span)` in `extractor/mod.rs`, plus a new `DiagnosticCode::SkippedCandidate` variant. Wire it into every malformed-but-matched arm in `alias.rs::classify_type_alias` and the end of each detector chain in `visit.rs` (lines 236-247, 262-293). This is a `crates/core/AGENTS.md` checklist requirement, not a lint — distinguishing "not this shape" from "this shape but unsupported" needs domain judgment per call site.

**Resolves:** `extractor-classify-type-alias-omit-pick-etc`, `extractor-extract-props-arg-terminal-none`, `extractor-failed-detector-silence`, `extractor-computed-property-keys`. New detector _coverage_ (anonymous default export, class components, `Object.assign`, class-expression components, `satisfies`) is a separate feature-gap task — `record_skip` only makes the existing miss visible, it doesn't add support.

**ADR:** No.

### 3. Pipeline discovery/merge diagnostic gaps

**Root cause:** Three independent bugs, not one mechanism. `discover_files` returns a bare `Vec<Utf8PathBuf>` with no diagnostic-return channel at all, so `walker.flatten()` silently drops every `ignore::Walk` error. `pipeline/mod.rs:220`'s empty-`src_dirs` guard (`!options.src_dirs.is_empty() && ...`) is a plain boolean logic error. `pipeline/mod.rs:386`'s `components.insert(key, entry)` discards the `Option<ComponentEntry>` return value that already reveals a collision — the data needed to diagnose it is sitting right there, unused.

**Mechanism `[corrected]`:** give `discover_files` a `&mut Vec<Diagnostic>` param, pushing on `Err` and on the non-UTF8-path fallback (reuse the pattern at `mod.rs:269-272`). Also update `discover_files`'s two direct test call sites (`mod.rs:542,562`, currently calling it with the old 2-arg signature). Fix the `mod.rs:220` guard with a _distinct diagnostic message_ for "no source directories were configured" vs. "the configured directories don't exist on disk" — dropping the `!is_empty()` conjunct alone routes an empty list into the "missing dirs" branch, which builds its message from `options.src_dirs.first()`/`.iter().join()` and would read as "None of the configured source directories exist: " with nothing after the colon, confusing for a genuinely-empty list. Check `components.insert`'s return at `mod.rs:386` and push a collision diagnostic on `Some(_)` — **this catches only a genuine 3+-way same-key collision, not the realistic 2-directory overlap case.** Tracing the actual keying logic: the disambiguation key is `format!("{} ({})", base_name, entry.file_path)` applied to every occurrence after the first, so with exactly two duplicate mappings from the same file (what `["./src", "./src/components"]`-style overlap actually produces via `component_mappings.extend()` with no dedup anywhere), the first gets the plain key and the second gets the disambiguated key — two _different_ keys, so `insert` never sees a collision. Overlapping `src_dirs` needs its own separate fix: dedup `src_files` by canonical path after sorting in `discover.rs` (e.g. `files.dedup()` post-sort), or dedup `component_mappings` by `(name, file_path)` before the keying loop in `mod.rs`. Implement both — the insert-return check for genuine key collisions, and the dedup for the overlap case — don't rely on either alone.

**Resolves:** `pipeline-permission-denied-files`, `pipeline-non-utf8-filenames`, `pipeline-empty-src-dirs`, `pipeline-same-name-same-file-collision`, `pipeline-overlapping-src-dirs`.

**ADR:** No.

### 4. No panic-containment boundary

**Root cause:** Zero `catch_unwind` anywhere in the repo (confirmed by grep). The three async NAPI entry points (`extract_all`, `extract_file_incremental`, `initialize_session`) are only panic-safe by _accident_ — they happen to run inside `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, whose `JoinError` catches the unwind as a side effect of tokio's own plumbing, not a decision anyone made. Because it was never written down anywhere, every later concurrent/cross-boundary addition reinvented the answer independently and got inconsistent results: `pipeline/mod.rs:260,357`'s rayon `.map()` closures have no per-item boundary at all; `plugin.rs`'s hook loop calls `plugin.on_x(...)` directly with zero isolation between plugins or from the pipeline invoking them; `crates/binding/src/lib.rs`'s `create_session`/`close_session` skip `spawn_blocking` entirely, missing even the accidental protection their siblings get; and `pipeline/watch.rs:93`'s `std::sync::Mutex` can poison permanently, specifically because the unprotected rayon batches and plugin hooks from the first two run while that lock is held.

**Mechanism `[corrected]`:** add `crates/core/src/panic_guard.rs`: `pub fn contain_panic<T>(label: &str, f: impl FnOnce() -> T) -> Result<T, Diagnostic>` (public, not `pub(crate)` — `crates/binding` needs to call it across the crate boundary), plus a new `DiagnosticCode::InternalPanic` variant. Wrap each rayon closure body in `pipeline/mod.rs:260,357`. Wrap each individual `plugin.on_x(...)` call in `plugin.rs`'s loops (not the whole loop, so one bad plugin degrades only itself, tagged with `plugin.name()`). Wrap `create_session`/`close_session` bodies in `crates/binding/src/lib.rs`, and have the other three NAPI entry points call it inside their existing `spawn_blocking` closures too, so their safety stops being incidental. Defense in depth: replace `watch.rs:93`'s `.expect("init lock poisoned")` with `.unwrap_or_else(|p| p.into_inner())`. Document the rule in `crates/core/AGENTS.md`.

**Verified correction — the plugin-hook wrapping needs an explicit `UnwindSafe` decision.** `plugin.rs`'s two hook calls (`on_file_extracted(file_path, &mut data)`, `on_component_resolved(&mut entry)`) each capture a `&mut` reference, and `&mut T` is unconditionally `!UnwindSafe` in std — `contain_panic`'s closure bound as originally drafted (`+ UnwindSafe`) will not compile against these call sites; this is a hard compiler error, not a style nit. Resolve it inside `contain_panic` itself, not at each call site: wrap the closure in `std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe` internally, with a documented rationale — this codebase's `SourceData`/`ComponentEntry` have no interior mutability (`Cell`/`RefCell`) that could leave an inconsistent, observably-torn state behind after a caught panic; the whole per-item operation is what gets abandoned, not a partial mutation trusted afterward. `AssertUnwindSafe` is safe to apply as a blanket internal implementation detail of `contain_panic` specifically because of that data-shape guarantee — state it in the function's doc comment so a future caller with genuine interior mutability doesn't inherit the assumption unknowingly. Also worth noting: `napi-rs` (the pinned version) has its own opt-in `#[napi(catch_unwind)]` attribute that wraps a function body in `catch_unwind` at the FFI boundary specifically — a viable complementary/alternative mechanism for the NAPI entry points worth considering alongside (or instead of) routing them through `contain_panic` by hand.

**Resolves:** P1-3, P1-4, P1-5, P1-9.

**ADR: Yes — see draft below.**

### 5. Unbounded allocation from input-derived size

**Root cause:** `extractor/mod.rs` already solved exactly this shape of problem once (`MAX_SOURCE_NESTING_DEPTH` / `max_bracket_nesting_depth`, with a doc comment explaining why) — nobody generalized or even cross-referenced that precedent when `template.rs`'s Cartesian-product loop or `lsp.rs`'s header parsing were written later. A discoverability gap, not a missing type.

**Mechanism:** Add `const MAX_TEMPLATE_LITERAL_EXPANSIONS: usize = 4096` checked inside `try_expand_template_literal`'s accumulation loop (`resolver/template.rs`), falling through to the existing Opaque+diagnostic path on overflow. Add `const MAX_LSP_MESSAGE_BYTES` gating the `vec![0u8; len]` allocation in `cli/commands/lsp.rs:36`. No shared function is practical across crates with different data shapes — add a code-review checklist line instead: "does this size come from parsed/protocol input, and is it capped before use?"

**Resolves:** P1-1, P1-2.

**ADR:** No.

### 6. LSP scaffold immaturity

**Root cause:** `lsp.rs` is a new, zero-test, hand-rolled JSON-RPC framing layer with no capability/handler consistency check — it advertises `hoverProvider: true` with no hover handler behind it, and a malformed header desyncs the stream instead of resyncing.

**Mechanism `[corrected]`:** don't advertise `hoverProvider: true` until a handler exists. The `content_length: None` branch's originally-proposed fix — "resync by consuming to the next blank line" — is **ineffective as stated**: tracing the actual control flow, the header-reading loop already reads and breaks on the blank line _before_ the `content_length: None` check runs, so "consume to the next blank line" would be a no-op against code that's already past that point. The real problem is structural: with no `Content-Length`, there is no way to know how many bytes the message body occupies, so it cannot be skip-consumed at all — the next read will misinterpret body bytes as new headers. Fix: treat a headerless/no-`Content-Length` message as unrecoverable and close or reset the connection with a diagnostic, rather than attempting to skip past it — LSP framing gives no other resync signal once this state is reached. Longer-term, consider `lsp-server`/`lsp-types` instead of hand-rolled framing.

**Resolves:** P1-6, P1-7.

**ADR:** No.

### 7. Extractor depth-tracking proxy mismatch

**Root cause:** `max_bracket_nesting_depth` bounds raw-text _bracket_ depth as a stand-in for AST recursion depth, but `ts_type_to_collected` recurses with no depth counter of its own — unlike the resolver's `resolve_*` functions, which already thread an explicit `depth: u8` parameter and bail past a limit. Chained conditional types achieve deep type-nesting with proportionally fewer brackets per level than paren/object nesting, so the proxy metric undercounts exactly the case it's meant to catch.

**Mechanism:** Thread a depth counter through `ts_type_to_collected` and sibling functions in `extractor/mod.rs`, bailing with a diagnostic past e.g. depth 500 — bringing the extractor into the same convention the resolver already established.

**Resolves:** P1-8.

**ADR:** No.

### 8. Resolver precedence: two hand-copied orderings

**Root cause:** `named.rs` documents "check source-defined types before known-pattern shortcuts" as intentional, with an explicit comment explaining why. `chain.rs`'s `extends`-clause path re-implements the same sequence independently — and gets the order backwards, checking known-pattern shortcuts first. Nothing ties the two orderings together, so `chain.rs` was free to drift the moment it was written, and nothing since has caught it. This is the confirmed, demonstrable bug from the original audit (P0-1).

**Mechanism:** extract the shared logic into `resolve_source_defined_or_known(...)` in `resolver/mod.rs` (or a new `resolver/precedence.rs`): fixed order `resolve_to_canonical → lookup_type_alias → lookup_interface → resolve_known`, taking closures for each call site's differing terminal handling (`Named` vs `ResolvedChain`). Both `named.rs` and `chain.rs` call it — reordering becomes structurally impossible. Add a regression fixture: a project-defined `interface SxProps` extended via `extends`, asserting the hardcoded MUI shortcut is _not_ substituted. Verified zero regression risk: no fixture or snapshot anywhere in the test suite exercises an `extends`-clause over a known-pattern name (`SxProps`, `SlotProps`, `VariantProps`, etc.), so this fix changes no currently-passing output.

**Verified correction — this fix does not fully unify the two functions.** `chain.rs` and `named.rs` diverge in two further respects beyond the P0-1 step that the shared function above doesn't address: `named.rs` checks React-builtin status _before_ canonical resolution, while `chain.rs` checks it _after_ the known-pattern block; and `chain.rs` checks `is_ts_utility_type` very early (before known-pattern), while `named.rs`'s analogous check runs last (after known-pattern _and_ after interface/alias lookup). Neither divergence reproduces the P0-1 bug shape (a user-defined interface being shadowed), so they're out of scope for this fix, but don't describe the two functions as "unified" once this lands — flag both as open follow-up items if a future audit revisits resolver precedence.

**Resolves:** P0-1.

**ADR:** No.

### 9. TOON truncation indicator dropped in one branch

**Root cause:** `LiteralUnion`'s truncate-with-`"...(+N)"` pattern was never factored into a helper. When `Union`/`Intersection` needed the same truncate-with-indicator behavior — in the _same function_, `format_type_compact` — the indicator half was dropped. This isn't code aging apart over time; it's proof the codebase has no mechanism that makes "format a truncated list" a single call site, even within one function.

**Mechanism:** Add `fn truncate_with_indicator(parts: &[String], limit: usize, sep: &str) -> String` in `toon.rs`. Route `LiteralUnion`, `Union`, and `Intersection` through it.

**Resolves:** P0-4. Cheapest fix in this document — all three call sites are already colocated.

**ADR:** No.

### 10. Schema hand-maintained separately from the real structs

**Root cause:** `cli/commands/schema.rs` hand-writes a JSON Schema as a `serde_json::json!()` literal instead of deriving it from `ComponentEntry`/`ExtractionStats`/`Diagnostic`. Every new field on those structs requires someone to remember to edit a second, structurally unrelated file — and the only existing test checks that the hand-written JSON is syntactically valid, never that it matches real serialized output, so drift is invisible to CI. Concrete drift already present: `.methods`/`.tags`, 5 of 9 `ExtractionStats` fields, and `.line`/`.column`/`.help` are all undocumented in the schema today.

**Mechanism `[corrected]`:** derive `schemars::JsonSchema` on the plain structs (`ComponentEntry`, `ParsedProp`, `ExtractionStats`, `Diagnostic`, `InheritedLayer`); call `schemars::schema_for!(ExtractionOutput)` from `cmd_schema()`. Hand-write `JsonSchema` impls only for `PropType` and `CollectedType` — the two enums that are actually recursive and actually have hand-written `Serialize` impls today, per ADR-0002. **Verified correction: `OpaqueReason` is not recursive and does not hand-write `Serialize`.** It has an ordinary `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]` with no self-referential field — ADR-0002's own text claims otherwise (asserting all three types hand-write their impl), and that ADR text is itself stale relative to the current code; the root-cause analysis originally propagated that stale claim without checking the source directly, exactly the kind of unverified inference this document is meant to avoid. `OpaqueReason` can derive `JsonSchema` normally, alongside the other plain structs — the fix is cheaper than originally stated. Flag ADR-0002's stale claim about `OpaqueReason` for a correction the next time that file is touched. If `schemars` as a new dependency is undesirable, the floor-level fix is a CI test that serializes a real fixture and validates it against `schema.rs`'s hand-written output.

**Resolves:** P0-5.

**ADR: Yes — see draft below.**

### 11. CLI exit-code contract has no shared type

**Root cause:** The 0/1/2 exit-code mapping is a doc-comment convention re-typed per command, not a shared function — `extract.rs:68-71` and `check.rs:21-30` already implement the same check with syntactically different code. `ExtractionOutput` has no `exit_code()` method, plausibly because `crates/core/AGENTS.md`'s "no terminal/display code in `crates/core`" rule got over-applied to mean "no exit-code logic belongs in core either." `cmd_watch` returns `()`, not `Result<i32>` (main.rs hardcodes exit 0 for that arm); `cmd_inspect` never touches `output.diagnostics` at all. Both were plausibly written by copying the general command-handler shape without copying the exit-code block, because nothing — return type, trait, lint — forces a new command handler to remember it.

**Mechanism `[corrected]`:** add `impl ExtractionOutput { pub fn max_severity(&self) -> Option<DiagnosticSeverity>; pub fn exit_code(&self, strict: bool) -> i32 }` in `core/types/output.rs` — pure data-in/data-out, same category as the existing `html_element()` helper, so it doesn't violate the core/no-terminal-code rule. **Verified gap: `DiagnosticSeverity` has no ordering today** (`#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)]`, no `Ord`/`PartialOrd`, no manual impl) — `max_severity()` needs one added before it can be implemented as a one-liner. Add `Ord`/`PartialOrd`/`Eq` (with variant declaration order double-checked against "worst severity wins" semantics — derived `Ord` ranks by declaration order, not by any inherent worst-to-best meaning) or a private `fn rank(&self) -> u8` helper used inside `max_severity()` instead of relying on derived `Ord`. Route `extract.rs` and `check.rs` through the new method (collapsing their inline checks) — note `check.rs` additionally supports a `--strict` warnings-escalate-to-1 path that `extract.rs`'s args have no equivalent flag for today; preserve that distinction rather than assuming the two commands' checks are fully identical. Change `cmd_watch` to return `Result<i32>` and call `exit_code(false)` after each pass, or explicitly gate propagation behind a `--ci` flag if always-0 is intentional for interactive use — document the choice either way instead of leaving it silent. Call `exit_code(false)` in `cmd_inspect` after a successful lookup so an Error diagnostic elsewhere in the tree surfaces even when the inspected component itself is fine.

**Resolves:** P3-1.

**ADR:** No — a doc comment on `exit_code()` documenting the mapping is sufficient; this formalizes an already-informal contract, it doesn't create a new one.

## Draft ADRs

Two clusters are genuine new architectural decisions, not enforcement of an existing pattern. Drafted here; write the real `docs/adr/000N-*.md` file as part of implementing that cluster, per the ADR guide's "write it when the decision is made" convention — these are proposals, not yet accepted.

### Proposed: 0005. Contain panics at a single, per-item boundary

**Context:** No existing ADR covers panic/unwind policy. Panic safety today is an accident of `tokio::spawn_blocking`'s `JoinError`, inconsistent across NAPI entry points, plugin hooks, and rayon batches — `create_session`/`close_session` don't even get that accidental protection, and `watch.rs`'s `std::sync::Mutex` can poison permanently as a direct consequence. Picking the wrong granularity now (per-batch vs. per-file vs. per-plugin) is expensive to fix retroactively once call sites depend on it.

**Decision:** Panics reachable from a rayon `.map()`, a `DocgenPlugin` hook, or a NAPI entry point are contained at per-file/per-plugin/per-call granularity through one sanctioned helper, `panic_guard::contain_panic`, converting the payload into a `Diagnostic` (or `napi::Error`) instead of aborting a batch, killing the whole pipeline, or poisoning a session lock. `contain_panic` wraps its closure in `AssertUnwindSafe` internally (documented rationale: this codebase's data has no interior mutability that could leave an observably-torn state behind a caught panic), so callers never need to reason about `UnwindSafe` themselves — including the plugin-hook call sites, whose `&mut` captures are otherwise `!UnwindSafe`. At the NAPI boundary specifically, `napi-rs`'s own opt-in `#[napi(catch_unwind)]` attribute is a viable complementary or alternative mechanism worth considering alongside `contain_panic`.

**Consequences:**

- One bad file, plugin, or session call degrades to a diagnostic instead of taking down everything sharing its batch/pipeline/session.
- Every future concurrent, plugin, or FFI entry point has one obvious place to route through, instead of re-deriving the answer.
- `watch.rs`'s poisoned-mutex trap becomes structurally much less likely, since nothing panics while the lock is held anymore.

### Proposed: 0006. Derive JSON Schema instead of hand-writing it

**Context:** `schema.rs`'s hand-written schema has already drifted from `ComponentEntry`/`ExtractionStats`/`Diagnostic`'s real fields, undetected because the only test checks JSON syntax validity, not field-set parity. ADR-0002 already established the precedent of hand-writing `Serialize` for the three recursive enums (`PropType`, `CollectedType`, `OpaqueReason`) to avoid a recursion-limit blowup.

**Decision:** Derive `schemars::JsonSchema` on the plain output structs, including `OpaqueReason` (verified non-recursive, already using an ordinary `derive` for `Serialize` — not one of the hand-written cases despite ADR-0002's text suggesting otherwise); hand-write matching `JsonSchema` impls only for `PropType` and `CollectedType`, the two enums that are actually recursive and actually hand-write `Serialize` today. `cmd_schema()` calls `schemars::schema_for!(ExtractionOutput)` instead of building a `json!()` literal by hand.

**Consequences:**

- A second hand-maintained trait impl per recursive enum whenever a variant is added — the same "compiler won't remind you" tradeoff ADR-0002 already accepted for `Serialize`, now doubled. Scoped to 2 enums (`PropType`, `CollectedType`), not 3.
- Every plain-struct field addition is schema-correct automatically; only the two recursive enums need manual attention going forward.
- New dependency (`schemars`) — if that's undesirable, the floor-level alternative is a CI test that serializes a real fixture and validates it against the hand-written schema, catching drift without adding a dependency.

7:## The 6-phase data flow
12:- **Phase 1 — discover.** `discover_files()` walks `src_dirs` via the `ignore` crate, filters to `.ts`/`.tsx`, applies built-in and user excludes, canonicalizes each path, then sorts and dedups. Sequential — it's I/O-bound directory walking, not CPU work worth parallelizing, and the final sort is required for the determinism invariant below.
13:- **Phase 2 — parse (parallel).** `src_files.par_iter().map(...)` via rayon. Each file either hits the `.d.ts` cache or gets parsed fresh by `extractor::parse_file`. This is the phase worth parallelizing: OXC parsing is pure CPU work, one file is fully independent of another, and this is typically the dominant cost of a run. Every closure body is wrapped in `panic_guard::contain_panic`.
14:- **Phase 3 — merge (+3.5/3.6), sequential.** Each file's `SourceData` (plus any plugin `on_file_extracted` mutation) is folded into one `GlobalSourceData` via hash-map insertions. This phase is sequential specifically because it's cheap (hash-map inserts, not real work) and because `GlobalSourceData` is a single shared structure being built incrementally — parallelizing it would require synchronization that costs more than the merge itself. Phase 3.5 (Full HTML-attribute mode) and Phase 3.6 (ambient TS lib files) extend the same merge with `@types/react` and `lib.es5.d.ts`/`lib.dom.d.ts`, both going through `merge_cached_dts_file` so their diagnostics aren't dropped (see Invariant 3).
15:- **Phase 4 — resolve (parallel).** `mappings.par_iter().map(|m| resolve_component(m, &ctx))`, again via rayon, again each closure wrapped in `contain_panic`. `ResolutionContext` wraps `Arc<GlobalSourceData>` so every thread reads the same immutable snapshot; per this crate's `AGENTS.md`, all resolver inputs must be owned or `Arc`-wrapped since rayon may run this on any thread.
16:- **Phase 5 — collect/dedup/serialize.** Sequential fold of `(ComponentEntry, Vec<Diagnostic>)` pairs into the output `BTreeMap`, running the display-name collision/disambiguation logic (Invariant 1) and each plugin's `on_component_resolved` hook, then persisting the DTS cache and building `ExtractionStats`.
18:**Why parallel exactly at phases 2 and 4, nowhere else:** those are the only two phases doing embarrassingly-parallel, side-effect-free-per-item CPU work over an already-known-size collection. Discovery is I/O-walk-bound: merge and collect both build one shared structure incrementally, which is cheaper done sequentially than synchronized.
20:## Watch mode's incremental model

67:## Invariants
73:3. **Every `.d.ts` merge into `GlobalSourceData` — main-loop, Full-mode `@types/react`, and ambient lib.d.ts — must drain the parsed file's own diagnostics before merging, because `GlobalSourceData` itself has no diagnostics field to catch them later.** Phase 3.5/3.6 route through the shared `merge_cached_dts_file` helper specifically to guarantee this; calling `global.merge()` directly on freshly-parsed data (as Phase 3.5/3.6 originally did) silently drops any excessive-nesting or parse-error diagnostic the extractor raised while parsing that file. 85:## Locked design decisions
87:- **Two rayon parallel phases, everything else sequential.** Already covered above under "the 6-phase data flow" — restated here because it's the decision most likely to look "obviously improvable" by parallelizing merge/collect too. Don't: both are cheap relative to parse/resolve, and both build one shared mutable structure whose synchronization cost would exceed the sequential cost.
88:- **DTS cache keys on `(path, size, mtime_ns)`, not a content hash.** A cheap stat-only check is the entire point of this cache's speed advantage; a content hash closes the residual staleness gap (Known Gaps below) but was deliberately rejected as disproportionate to the problem's real frequency — see `cache.rs:196-204`'s doc comment and `docs/root-cause-analysis.md` line 140, which additionally notes that _if_ this is ever revisited, a fast non-cryptographic hash (xxhash/CRC) over bytes already being read for size would be the right scope, not a full cryptographic hash.
90:- **`ComponentMapping`/`GlobalSourceData` construction happens once per cold run and is reused, immutable, across all of Phase 4's parallel resolve closures via `Arc`.** `ResolutionContext::new(global.clone(), options)` wraps the `Arc<GlobalSourceData>` once outside the `par_iter()`, not per-item — this is the mechanism that makes "all resolver inputs must be owned or `Arc`-wrapped" (crates/core/AGENTS.md) actually cheap rather than merely correct.
93:## Known gaps
108:- **DTS cache mtime+size staleness on coarse-resolution filesystems** (`docs/edge-cases.md` P0-2, `docs/root-cause-analysis.md` line 140). An edit landing in the same tick as a prior write _and_ producing an identical file length is served a stale cache hit. Scoped to `.d.ts` files only; not recommended for immediate action per the root-cause doc — see the Locked Design Decisions entry above for what a future fix should look like if ever revisited.
109:- **`ReverseDeps` is not incrementally updated within a watch session.** Only structural changes (a new `WatchSession`, i.e. restarting) rebuild it; adding or removing an import inside an existing file during a session leaves the reverse graph stale for that edge until the session restarts. 176:1. **Structured, typed degradation diagnostics.** Running this tool across all 21 fixture libraries produces **82 diagnostics** with typed codes (`UNRESOLVABLE_IMPORT`: 30, `OPAQUE_TYPE`: 29, `INDEXED_ACCESS_OPAQUE`: 19, `DISCRIMINATED_UNION`: 2, `TEMPLATE_LITERAL_OPAQUE`: 2), file/line context, and human-readable help text (e.g. _"Enable typescript-go to resolve indexed access types."_). Neither RDT nor react-docgen tell you _why_ a prop came out wrong or missing — they silently omit it or print a generic parse error. This tool's non-negotiable #6 ("always emit a Diagnostic when degrading, never fail silently," `AGENTS.md`) makes every gap in the tables above something a consumer's tooling can detect and act on, not something discovered by manually diffing output.
177:2. **`.d.ts`-only fixtures.** 8 of the 55 fixture files in this corpus (`mui`, `chakra`, `mantine`, `radix`, `react-aria`) are declaration-only — real published library type definitions with no accompanying `.tsx` source. **Neither RDT nor react-docgen can run on these at all** (both need a real component implementation to parse). This tool extracts full prop tables from them today — the reason it can validate against `node_modules`-vendored third-party types, not just first-party source.
179:4. **Cross-package monorepo import resolution** (`ImportResolutionMap`, barrel/re-export chain following, `extra_paths` workspace aliasing). RDT resolves within a single `ts.Program`'s file set — following a monorepo's package boundaries means configuring that whole program correctly. This tool's import resolution is a first-class, independently-tested layer (`import_map.rs`, `resolver/import.rs`).
180:5. **Machine-consumable structured types**, not stringified type names. This tool's `PropType` is a real tagged union (`union`, `literalUnion`, `array`, `intersection`, `eventHandler`, ...) serialized as JSON — a consumer can programmatically ask "is this a union of string literals" without parsing a type string. RDT and react-docgen both hand back a printed type string (or, for react-docgen, a partial tagged shape with a `.raw` escape hatch) as the primary representation.
181:6. **A `composes` field that actually gets populated.** `ComponentEntry.composes` is react-docgen's own documented mechanism for "these props come from a type we're not flattening — here's its name/expression" — but it sat unused for the type-checker-boundary failures above until this report found and fixed it. `base-ui/MenuTrigger` and all 3 `headlessui/Listbox` components now surface their real unresolvable expression (a mapped type, two conditional types) through `composes` in RDT-format output, instead of silently returning zero props with no trace. Not a fix for the underlying gap: 6 of the 10 outlier components (Ariakit, `ark-ui`, `storybook-emotion`, `fluentui`) still show empty `composes` — their failure happens further upstream (generic-alias substitution not matching the pattern at all) than the one dead end this closed.
185:## Shortcomings and remediation plan
189:### Already tracked, deferred pending a real type checker (Corsa/`typescript-go`)
191:Confirmed still accurate against current code during this report — see `docs/type-checker-integration.md` and `docs/STATUS.md`:
193:- **Generic type-parameter substitution through multi-level type-alias chains.** Root-caused here for the `ariakit`/`ark-ui` outliers above: Ariakit's own `Props<T, O> = O & Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>, keyof O>` pattern requires substituting a generic param (`T = "button"`) through a nested `Omit`+`ComponentPropsWithoutRef` chain — exactly the "generic parameter substitution" item already listed as Corsa-deferred. This report adds concrete evidence (4+ real-world outlier components in one corpus) that this isn't a theoretical gap.
194:- **`@emotion/styled`'s two-arg `styled(tag, options)<T>(fn)` overload** (`storybook-emotion/Button` — already `docs/rdt-coverage.md`'s open gap #2). RDT needs a type checker for this too — not a competitive gap.
